passage: In the art room, Amandeep tore the corner off his drawing and shoved his chair back so hard it screeched. Jatin Sir looked up from his desk. "I'm furious with both of them," Amandeep blurted out. "They are wrecking our home." His fists were shaking. Jatin Sir did not tell him to calm down. He slid a fresh sheet and a thick black marker across the desk. "Draw how it feels." Amandeep scribbled hard until the paper nearly tore. Then his hand slowed. "Underneath, I'm just sad," he said, and his voice cracked. Jatin Sir said he could tell the school counsellor too, and his mother, when he was ready.

qa.q: What did Amandeep tear in the art room?
qa.a: He tore the corner off his drawing.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's remark "Underneath, I'm just sad" suggest about his anger?
qa.a: It suggests the anger was covering sadness about his parents, which came out once he began drawing his feelings.

qa.q: What helpful outlets did Jatin Sir offer for the anger?
qa.a: He gave him a fresh sheet and a marker to draw how it felt and suggested telling the school counsellor and his mother when ready.

qa.q: How might Jatin Sir see Amandeep's outburst?
qa.a: He seems to see it as a boy's pain rather than bad behaviour, since he did not tell him to calm down but gave him a way to express it.

grounding: A child angry at both parents in a school setting says it in words and drawing and finds the sadness underneath.

passage:
"Aadhya, your Francis Uncle was once the angriest boy in Bandra. When my parents split up, I was eleven. I was furious with both of them for wrecking our home.
I slammed doors so hard the pictures shook. One day I shouted at my mother, 'It's all your fault!' It wasn't true. I saw her face crumple, and I felt worse than before.
My grandfather took me out running along the sea wall every morning after that. 'Run it off,' he said. 'Then tell me in words.' Slowly I learned to say, 'I'm angry because I'm sad.' That was the truth underneath."

qa.q: Where did young Francis run with his grandfather?
What was young Francis feeling underneath his anger?
qa.a: He was sad about his family breaking up, and the fury was covering that sadness.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Francis handle his anger?
qa.a: Running with his grandfather every morning and learning to say in words that he was angry because he was sad.

qa.q: How did Francis's mother react when he blamed her?
qa.a: Her face crumpled, showing she was deeply hurt by his unfair words.

grounding: An uncle recalls being angry at both parents after their split, slamming doors and unfairly blaming one, then learning to run and say the sadness in words.

passage:
Moving day was chaos. It was pouring, the van was late, and half the boxes were still open. Akash's mother, Rekha, was on the phone with the landlord.
Akash kicked a box of books. It split and the books slid out. "This is all your fault!" he shouted, then stopped. It wasn't only hers.
Rekha put the phone down. "Say it, Akash. Say what you really feel."
His throat hurt. "I'm angry at both of you. You broke our home. And I'm sad."
She hugged him. "That's allowed."
Then she gave him a notebook and a pen. "Draw it while I finish the call." He drew a house with a crack down the middle.

qa.q: What was Akash really feeling on moving day?
qa.a: He was angry at both parents, and underneath that anger he was sad about losing their home.

qa.q: What helped Akash express his anger safely?
qa.a: Rekha asked him to say what he felt in words and gave him a notebook to draw it.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Akash blamed her?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt hurt and stressed, but she stayed calm and helped him say the truth.

grounding: On a chaotic moving day a boy lashes out and unfairly blames his mother, then puts his anger and sadness into words and a drawing.
